askBook: What can I use from {name} in my training right now?
askMind: What would {name} tell me to do in my training right now?
promptNote: Ground training advice in these sources and say whose idea you're using. Creators are for motivation and ideas; the science and coaches come first. Always adapt to their age.

items.name: Strength Training for Young Athletes
items.by: William J. Kraemer & Steven J. Fleck
items.big: Strength training is safe and great for young athletes when it's supervised and technique comes first.
ideas: Learn the movement with light weight or bodyweight before adding load.
Progress slowly: small increases, good form on every rep.
Adult supervision and proper equipment make youth training safe.
Stronger muscles and tendons help prevent sports injuries.
items.use: Use it as the foundation for how you train at your age.

items.name: Starting Strength
items.big: A few big barbell lifts, done well and made heavier slowly, build real strength.
ideas: Squat, deadlift, press and bench press cover most of the body.
Add a little weight each session while form stays perfect.
Technique is learned: film yourself and fix one thing at a time.
items.use: Use it later, with a coach, when you move to barbell training.
items.note: Barbell lifts at your age: only with a coach or adult watching, and never max attempts.

items.name: The Muscle and Strength Pyramid: Training
items.by: Eric Helms, Andy Morgan & Andrea Valdez
items.big: Get the big things right first: consistency, then volume and effort, then the small details.
ideas: Adherence at the bottom: a plan you actually follow beats a perfect plan.
Then volume, intensity and frequency; then progression; then exercise choice; then rest times and tempo.
Don't major in the minors.
items.use: Use it to know what really matters in training and what doesn't.

items.name: Science and Development of Muscle Hypertrophy
items.big: Muscle grows from hard sets close to failure, enough weekly volume, and progress over time.
ideas: Mechanical tension is the main driver of muscle growth.
A wide range of reps (about 6-30) builds muscle if sets are hard.
Train each muscle about twice a week.
items.use: Use it when you want the science behind building muscle.

items.name: Scientific Principles of Hypertrophy Training
items.by: Mike Israetel, James Hoffmann, Melissa Davis & Jared Feather
items.big: Every muscle has a range of weekly sets: too few doesn't grow, too many can't be recovered from.
ideas: Volume landmarks: minimum effective volume up to maximum recoverable volume.
Build up sets over a few weeks, then deload to recover.
Pick exercises you can feel working and progress over time.
items.use: Use it when planning how many sets to do per week.

items.name: Built from Broken
items.big: Joints and tendons get stronger too, if you train them on purpose.
ideas: Tendons adapt slower than muscles: build up gradually.
Train full range of motion, including end ranges, to protect joints.
Small daily 'joint prep' work prevents big injuries.
items.use: Use it if something aches (knees from basketball, for example) and to stay injury-free.

items.name: Becoming a Supple Leopard
items.big: Good positions and daily mobility work let you move and perform better.
ideas: Organize your spine and joints before you lift or jump.
Spend about 10 minutes a day on mobility for tight spots.
Pain is a signal to fix position, not to push through.
items.use: Use it to fix tight hips, ankles or shoulders.

items.name: Back Mechanic
items.big: A strong, stable core protects your back; learn to move from the hips.
ideas: The 'Big 3': curl-up, side plank and bird dog.
Hinge at the hips and keep a neutral spine when lifting things.
Avoid repeated heavy spine bending.
items.use: Use it to keep your back healthy for life.

items.name: Convict Conditioning
items.big: You can get very strong with bodyweight alone by following step-by-step progressions.
ideas: Six big moves: push-ups, squats, pull-ups, leg raises, bridges, handstand push-ups.
Each has 10 steps from easy to very hard.
Master each step before moving on.
items.use: Use it to get strong at home with no equipment.

items.name: Overcoming Gravity
items.big: A complete, careful system for gymnastics and calisthenics strength.
ideas: Plan progressions for skills like handstands, muscle-ups and levers.
Build tendon strength slowly to avoid elbow and wrist injuries.
items.use: Use it for calisthenics skills once the basics are solid.

items.name: Training for the Uphill Athlete
items.by: Steve House, Scott Johnston & Kilian Jornet
items.big: Build a big aerobic base with lots of easy hours, then add hills and strength for the mountains.
ideas: Most training should be easy enough to talk (zone 1-2).
Muscular endurance: long uphill work with a pack.
Increase weekly hours gradually, about 10% at a time.
items.use: Use it to get ready for Patagonia, Peru, the Alps and other mountain trips.

items.name: Endure
items.big: Your brain sets limits before your body really runs out.
ideas: Belief and motivation change how hard effort feels.
Smiling and positive self-talk can make hard work feel easier.
items.use: Use it to push through the last minutes of a hard hike or game.

items.name: Outlive
items.big: Train now for the body you want at 80: strength, stability and a big aerobic engine.
ideas: Zone 2 cardio (easy but steady) builds the base; some hard intervals raise your top end.
Strength and balance protect you for life.
Sleep and good food are part of training.
items.use: Use it to understand why training every day matters for your whole life.

items.name: Why We Sleep
items.big: Sleep is when your body and brain recover and grow.
ideas: Teenagers need about 8-10 hours of sleep.
Regular sleep and wake times matter as much as total hours.
Screens and caffeine late at night hurt sleep.
items.use: Use it to take sleep as seriously as training.
items.note: Some numbers in the book have been debated by scientists; the core message (sleep matters a lot) is solid.

items.name: The Mamba Mentality
items.big: Kobe's approach: obsessive preparation, studying the game, and loving the work.
ideas: Watch film of yourself and the best players to learn.
Master the fundamentals until they're automatic.
Prepare your body: strength and recovery were part of his daily routine.
items.use: Use it for basketball and for the discipline to train every day.

items.name: Relentless
items.big: The trainer of Jordan and Kobe on what makes the greatest competitors different.
ideas: Great competitors keep going when everyone else stops.
Control your emotions under pressure.
Be obsessed with getting better, not with being praised.
items.use: Use it for mental toughness in sports and business.
items.note: Very intense in tone. Take the drive, not the idea that you must never rest: recovery matters.

items.name: Jump Attack
items.big: A structured program to jump higher using strength and explosive training.
ideas: Build strength first, then add explosive jumps.
Quality over quantity: every jump at full effort, with good landings.
items.use: Use it for dunking goals, carefully and with good landing technique.

items.name: Range
items.big: Trying many sports and skills when young builds better athletes and thinkers.
ideas: Most top athletes played many sports as kids before specializing.
Variety builds coordination and prevents overuse injuries.
It's fine not to know your one thing yet.
items.use: Use it to feel good about playing basketball and doing lots of other sports.

items.name: Peak
items.big: Experts are made by deliberate practice: focused work on weaknesses with feedback.
ideas: Practice just outside your comfort zone.
Get fast feedback (a coach, video) and fix one thing at a time.
Hours alone don't make you great; focused hours do.
items.use: Use it to improve skills like shooting or dribbling faster.

items.name: The Champion's Mind
items.big: The mental habits of champions: confidence, focus and handling pressure.
ideas: Focus on the process you control, not the result.
Use a short routine before shots or big moments.
Talk to yourself like a coach, not a critic.
items.use: Use it before games and tryouts.

items.name: Mindset
items.big: Believing you can improve (a growth mindset) makes you improve more.
ideas: Abilities grow with effort, strategy and help from others.
Mistakes are information, not proof you're bad at something.
Praise effort and strategy, not talent.
items.use: Use it whenever something feels too hard: 'not yet' instead of 'can't'.

items.name: Spark
items.big: Exercise makes your brain sharper, happier and better at learning.
ideas: Cardio before studying can boost focus.
Exercise reduces stress and improves mood.
items.use: Use it as a reason to work out before homework.

items.name: Atomic Habits
items.big: Tiny improvements, done every day, add up to huge results.
ideas: Make training obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying.
Never miss twice: one missed workout is fine, two starts a new habit.
Identity: 'I'm an athlete who trains every day.'
items.use: Use it to never skip your daily workout.

items.name: Can't Hurt Me
items.big: When you think you're done, you're only about 40% done.
ideas: Callous your mind by doing hard things on purpose.
Take an honest look in the mirror: own your weaknesses.
Keep a 'cookie jar' of past wins to remember in hard moments.
items.use: Use it for mental toughness.
items.note: Goggins trained through serious injuries. Don't copy his extremes: pain that is sharp or in a joint means stop.

items.name: Food Rules
items.big: Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.
ideas: Eat real food, mostly things your grandparents would recognize.
Eat lots of plants, plus good protein.
Enjoy meals with family, slowly.
items.use: Use it for simple, healthy eating without dieting.

items.name: Dr. Mike Israetel
items.big: Train hard enough, with enough volume, and recover well: that's the whole game.
ideas: Stimulus, fatigue, recovery: balance all three.
Most sets should end 1-3 reps from failure.
Deload every few weeks.

items.name: Brad Schoenfeld
items.big: Many rep ranges build muscle when sets are hard.
ideas: Twice a week per muscle beats once.
Full range of motion usually works best.

items.name: Eric Helms
items.big: Consistency is the foundation; details come last.
ideas: Progress slowly and sustainably.
Natural athletes should set realistic expectations and be patient.

items.name: Stuart McGill
items.big: Stiffen the core to move the limbs: protect your back for life.
ideas: The Big 3 exercises daily.
Train the core to resist movement, not only to create it.

items.name: Kelly Starrett
items.big: Ten minutes of mobility a day keeps your body moving well.
ideas: Test and retest: try a mobility drill and see if you move better.
Sleep, walking and good positions are recovery tools.

items.name: Andrew Huberman
items.big: Morning sunlight and regular sleep times set your body clock.
ideas: Get outside light soon after waking.
Keep bedtime and wake time steady, even on weekends.
Exercise and sleep are the biggest levers for health.
items.note: Skip his supplement talk at your age: food, sleep and training are enough.

items.name: Peter Attia
items.big: Build strength, stability and aerobic fitness now for a long, active life.
ideas: Zone 2 cardio as a base.
Grip strength and balance matter more than people think.

items.name: Tim Grover
items.by: Trainer of Michael Jordan and Kobe Bryant
items.big: The greatest competitors are relentless about the work nobody sees.
ideas: Train your body so your skills hold up in the fourth quarter.
Be comfortable being uncomfortable.

items.name: Mark Rippetoe
items.big: Strong people are harder to kill and more useful in general.
ideas: Learn the big lifts with perfect form.
Add a little weight regularly.

items.name: Joe DeFranco
items.big: Athletes need strength, speed, mobility and conditioning together.
ideas: His 'Limber 11' is a quick mobility routine for athletes.
Train to be athletic, not just to look strong.

items.name: Kobe Bryant
items.big: Love the process so much that the hard work feels like play.
ideas: Famous for training before sunrise.
Studied film of himself and of legends to learn.
Mastered one move at a time until it was perfect.

items.name: Michael Jordan
items.big: Failure is part of success: he missed thousands of shots and kept shooting.
ideas: Was cut from his high school varsity team and used it as fuel.
Competed hard in every practice, not just games.
items.fun: Didn't make his high school varsity team as a sophomore.

items.name: Stephen Curry
items.big: Skill comes from thousands of focused reps, and small players can change the game.
ideas: Rebuilt his shot as a teenager, even though it was hard.
Uses creative drills that train vision and handling at the same time.
Was told he was too small; proved everyone wrong with skill.

items.name: LeBron James
items.big: Take care of your body like a business: recovery is training.
ideas: Prioritizes 8-10 hours of sleep.
Invests heavily in recovery, mobility and nutrition to play for 20+ years.

items.name: Eliud Kipchoge
items.big: No human is limited. Discipline is doing what you should, even when you don't feel like it.
ideas: Consistency over years: he keeps a simple, steady routine.
Logs every training session in a notebook.
Trains hard but mostly smart and easy.

items.name: Kilian Jornet
items.big: Enjoy the mountains; fitness comes from spending lots of time moving in them.
ideas: Huge amounts of easy uphill movement build mountain fitness.
Listen to your body and respect the mountain.

items.name: David Goggins
items.big: When your mind says you're done, you still have more in you.
ideas: Do something hard every day to build mental toughness.
Hold yourself accountable honestly.
items.note: Don't copy his extremes. Sharp pain or joint pain means stop and rest.

items.name: Jeff Nippard
items.big: Train with the research on your side: the most effective exercises and set ranges, explained simply.
ideas: Pick exercises that stretch the muscle under load.
Progressive overload: add a rep or a little weight over time.
Most people need more consistency, not more exercises.
items.fun: Studied biochemistry and competed as a natural powerlifter and bodybuilder.

items.name: Jeremy Ethier
items.big: Clear, evidence-based workouts, including great ones you can do at home.
ideas: Good form and full range beat heavy ego lifting.
Home workouts can build muscle if you progress them.

items.name: Jeff Cavaliere (Athlean-X)
items.big: Train like an athlete, and fix imbalances before they become injuries.
ideas: Balance pushing with pulling to protect your shoulders.
Build strength and athleticism together.
items.fun: Was the head physical therapist and strength coach for the New York Mets.

items.name: Will Tennyson
items.big: Fitness can be fun: he tries famous athletes' diets and workouts and shows what really happens.
ideas: Make training and eating well something you enjoy.
Sees for himself what works rather than believing hype.
items.note: Some videos show huge eating challenges or strict diets: entertainment, not a plan for you.

items.name: Hampton Liu (Hybrid Calisthenics)
items.big: Anyone can start from zero with bodyweight training, one easy step at a time.
ideas: Start with the easiest version and progress when it feels good.
Kind, positive self-talk keeps you training.
Great beginner routines with no equipment.

items.name: Aaron Horschig (Squat University)
items.big: Move well before you move heavy.
ideas: Test your ankle and hip mobility.
Fix the cause of pain, not only the spot that hurts.

items.name: David Laid
items.big: Started lifting as a skinny teenager and documented years of steady progress.
ideas: Consistency over years beats any shortcut.
Enjoy the process of getting a little better every month.
items.fun: Began training around 14 and became famous for his transformation videos.
items.note: His physique took many years; compare yourself to your own past, not to him.

items.name: Chris Bumstead (CBum)
items.big: Discipline, patience and mental health all matter on the way to your goals.
ideas: Show up even on bad days.
Talks openly about mental health, which is part of being strong.
items.note: A pro bodybuilder's body is not a goal for a teenager. Take the discipline, not the physique target.
